audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final stress (final stress) rests on the best available description, Vazquez Alvarez 2011 (519-pp UT Austin reference-grammar dissertation by a native-speaker linguist), whose s.2.2 p.43 and s.9.6.1 p.284 statements I re-read verbatim in the PDF, with independent confirmation in Vazquez Alvarez 2002 pp.5-7 (explicit 2-6-syllable final-stress paradigm) and Coon 2010 p.190; Coon 2017 is silent; Bennett 2016:495-497 places Ch'ol with the Greater Tseltalan final-stress languages and adds only the family-wide caveat that reported phrasal stress shifts may be intonational -- already covered by the record's fences (interrogative initial shift = intonation; clitic-inclusive domain). No instrumental study of Ch'ol word stress exists as far as Crossref/Bennett's survey show. Nothing found suggests a reclassify. The weakness is clerical, not evidential: the exported catalog rec

sources.citation: Vázquez Álvarez, Juan Jesús. 2011. A Grammar of Chol, a Mayan Language. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin. (copied from the 2026-08-30 download of the chol.lingspace.org mirror)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In general, there is a main lexical stress in Chol which commonly falls on the last syllable of the word' (p.43); examples já', ja'ál, pixól, tyumúty, alaxáx, kixtyañúj, matye'chityám, buch-ul-oñ=tyo=ku=lá all final; compounds final with weak stress on first member (p.44); yes/no questions shift main stress to the first syllable (p.45, p.284: 'in a pragmatically neutral form, the stress in Chol falls on the last syllable of the word').

sources.citation: Vázquez Álvarez, Juan Jesús. 2002. Morfología del verbo de la lengua chol de Tila, Chiapas. Tesis de maestría, CIESAS, México. 411 PDF pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'El acento en el chol recae en la última sílaba de la palabra.' Paradigm wäy-él / wäy-äl-óñ / wäy-äl-oñ-lá / wäy-äl-oñ-bi-lá / wäy-äl-oñ-bi-ka-lá (2-6 syllables, all final). 'Sin embargo, el hablante puede darle mayor énfasis acentual a la primera sílaba cuando se interroga' (búch-ul 'Está sentado?').

sources.quote: After describing Q'anjob'al phrasal stress (initial phrase-medially, final phrase-finally): 'Similar patterns have been noted for Greater Tseltalan languages (Kaufman 1971, Attinasi 1973, Warkentin & Brend 1974, Haviland 1981, Coon 2010, Vázquez Álvarez 2011, Polian 2013)...'; notes some putative phrase-level stress in final-stress Mayan languages 'may involve phrase-level intonational contours rather than true word-level stress'. Phonemic stress reported only for Chontal, not Ch'ol.
